tips.title: Du, de la: "some"
body: French needs a little word before food and drink even where English has none: du pain (some bread), de l'eau (some water).
Du is for masculine nouns, de la for feminine ones, and de l' before a vowel.

tips.title: Le and la: every noun is masculine or feminine
body: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and "the" changes to match: le for masculine, la for feminine, l' before a vowel.
"My" changes too: mon for masculine, ma for feminine. Learn each noun with its le or la.

tips.title: Adjectives match the noun
body: Describing words agree with the noun: add -e for feminine and -s for plural. Grand becomes grande, petit becomes petite.
The added -e makes the last consonant heard: petit ("puh-tee"), petite ("puh-teet").

tips.title: J'ai faim: French "has" hunger
body: Where English says "I am hungry", French says "I have hunger": j'ai faim. The same goes for sleepy, thirsty, cold and your age.
So use avoir, not être, for these.

tips.title: Je veux + a verb
body: To say you want to do something, put the verb in its dictionary form (ending in -er, -ir or -re) after je veux.
On is a very common way to say "we": on mange (we're eating).

tips.title: Saying no: ne … pas
body: French wraps the verb in two words: ne before it, pas after it. Ne becomes n' before a vowel: je n'ai pas.
After pas, "a" and "some" become de: je n'ai pas de frère (I don't have a brother).

tips.title: J'aime le chocolat: keep the "the"
body: When you talk about liking things in general, French keeps le, la or les: j'aime le chocolat, tu aimes les chiens ?
J'adore is stronger than j'aime.

tips.title: Three ways to ask a question
body: In conversation, just raise your voice at the end: tu as quel âge ?
Est-ce que at the start also turns a sentence into a question, and qu'est-ce que means "what". Swapping the verb and subject (comment allez-vous ?) is more formal.

tips.title: Telling someone what to do
body: For instructions, drop the tu: tu tournes becomes tourne (turn), tu vas becomes va (go).
With vous it stays the same: tournez, allez.

tips.title: À for cities, en / au for countries
body: Use à with cities: j'habite à Lyon.
With countries, use en for feminine ones (en France), au for masculine ones (au Canada) and aux for plural ones (aux États-Unis). "From" is de, du or des: je viens des États-Unis.

tips.title: Je voudrais: a softer "I want"
body: Je veux can sound blunt with staff. Je voudrais ("I would like") is the polite way to order or ask.
Pour moi, … ("for me, …") also works when ordering.

tips.title: Je me lève: verbs you do to yourself
body: Some verbs take me, te or se because you do them to yourself: se lever (to get up), se doucher (to shower), s'habiller (to get dressed).
The little word goes before the verb: je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève.

tips.title: The past: j'ai mangé, je suis allé
body: The everyday past (passé composé) is avoir + the past participle: j'ai mangé, j'ai regardé.
Verbs of movement and staying, and verbs with se, use être instead, and the participle matches the subject: je suis allé (man), je suis allée (woman).

tips.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event
body: The imparfait sets the scene: what was going on or used to happen (elle habitait, elle allait). The passé composé tells the event (elle a trouvé).
Fairy tales use a literary past you'll only read: ils vécurent (they lived).

tips.title: Had done: avait / était + participle
body: To say something had already happened before another past event, use the imparfait of avoir or être plus the participle: il était déjà parti (he had already left).
Pendant que (while) takes the imparfait for the longer action.

tips.title: Plans: aller + verb, and si + present
body: Je vais + a verb is the everyday future: je vais réserver (I'm going to book).
With si (if) about a real possibility, use the present: s'il pleut, on reste (if it rains, we'll stay). Si becomes s' before il.

tips.title: J'ai mal à…: saying what hurts
body: Avoir mal à + the body part says where it hurts: j'ai mal à la tête (my head hurts). À + le contracts to au: j'ai mal au dos.
Depuis (since) with the present says how long: j'ai de la fièvre depuis hier.

tips.title: Giving advice: tu devrais, à ta place, il faut que
body: Tu devrais + verb is "you should". À ta place ("in your place") and si j'étais toi ("if I were you") take the conditional: j'irais, je dirais.
After il faut que or c'est important que, the next verb goes into the subjunctive: tu dors becomes que tu dormes.

tips.title: A été annulé: the passive
body: To say what was done to something, use être + the past participle, matching the noun: mon vol a été annulé, ma réservation a été annulée.
Conversation often uses on instead: on a annulé mon vol.

tips.title: Je pense que… / Je ne pense pas que…
body: Je pense que (I think that) is followed by the normal present: je pense que tu as raison.
When you doubt or deny it, use the subjunctive: je ne pense pas que ce soit juste.

tips.title: Linking ideas
body: D'un côté … de l'autre (on the one hand … on the other) balances two points.
Même si (even if) takes the normal present, unlike bien que (although), which takes the subjunctive: bien que ce soit difficile.

tips.title: Tu or vous?
body: Vous is for strangers, older people, customers and anyone at work you don't know well. It's also the plural "you". Tu is for friends, family, children and people your age.
Wait for the other person to suggest tu: on peut se tutoyer ?

tips.title: Extra-polite requests
body: The conditional softens any request: pourriez-vous (could you), auriez-vous (would you have), je vous serais reconnaissant (I would be grateful).
Swapping the verb and subject (pourriez-vous) also sounds more formal than tu peux.

tips.title: How people really talk: dropping ne
body: In everyday speech the ne of ne … pas usually disappears: c'est pas cher, je sais pas, which often sounds like chais pas.
Tu also shrinks to t' before a vowel: t'as vu ?, t'inquiète. Keep the full forms for writing.

tips.title: Culture: dating in France
body: French people rarely talk about "dating" as a stage: you meet through friends, go for a drink (boire un verre), and things move on from there without much labeling.
Compliments tend to be understated and specific (ton style, ton sourire) rather than effusive. A simple "c'est gentil" is the natural thank-you.
Friends greet each other with la bise (a kiss on each cheek); a first meeting in a romantic context often starts with it too.

tips.title: Culture: texting in France
body: Texts are short and full of abbreviations: mdr (mort de rire, LOL), dsl (désolé, sorry), dispo (disponible, free), and the ne of ne…pas almost always disappears.
"Coucou" is the friendly hello for friends and dates. English loanwords like matcher, ghoster and le feeling are everyday app slang.
Splitting the bill (on partage) is common on dates, though some still offer to pay the first time.

tips.title: Culture: meeting the family
body: Meeting the parents usually means things are serious. Use vous with them until they suggest tu.
Bring a small gift (une petite attention): flowers, chocolates or a good dessert. Wine is fine, but some hosts already have it planned.
Sunday lunch can last for hours. Offering to help clear the table (débarrasser) is always appreciated.

tips.title: Culture: la séduction à la française
body: Flirting in France tends to be subtle and witty: a lingering conversation, a well-chosen compliment, a bit of humor, rather than big declarations.
Compliments about someone's style, laugh or taste land better than comments about their body.
Catcalling (le harcèlement de rue) is not charming and is actually an offense in France. Flirting happens in conversation, not from across the street.

tips.title: Culture: humor and second degré
body: Teasing is often second degré (tongue-in-cheek): you say something with a straight face, and the other person knows you're joking.
A cheesy phrase d'accroche (pick-up line) only works if you obviously don't take it seriously. Laughing at it together is the point.
Keep teasing light and mutual; if they don't tease back, ease off.

tips.title: Culture: clear and respectful
body: Asking for someone's number (ton numéro) or suggesting a drink is perfectly normal. If they hesitate, take the hint gracefully.
A polite exit ("pas de souci, c'était sympa de discuter") keeps things friendly.
In texts, "bonjour toi" (morning, you) is a soft, affectionate opener.

tips.title: Culture: greetings in the French-speaking world
body: Always start with "Bonjour" (plus "madame" or "monsieur"): in a shop, to a bus driver, before asking anything. Skipping it is the classic mistake that makes people seem rude.
La bise: usually two kisses in most of France, three or even four in some regions, one in Belgium, three in Switzerland. In Québec people kiss less often, and hugs are common.
Gestures: pulling down your lower eyelid ("mon œil !") means "I don't believe you". A shrug with "bof" means "meh". When counting, the French start with the thumb.
In West Africa, greetings take time: ask about the family and the day before getting to business, and shake hands with your right hand.

tips.title: Culture: at the table in French
body: In France, lunch is around noon to 2 and dinner around 8. In Québec, Belgium and Switzerland the meals are "déjeuner, dîner, souper": breakfast, lunch, dinner. So "dîner" there is lunch!
Keep your hands on the table (wrists resting on the edge), not in your lap. Bread goes on the tablecloth next to your plate.
Tap water is free: ask for "une carafe d'eau". Service is included in French prices ("service compris"), so a tip is kind but optional. In Québec, tip about 15%.

tips.title: Culture: holidays in French-speaking places
body: In early January, the galette des rois is cut into slices: whoever finds the little charm (la fève) wears the paper crown. You can wish people "bonne année" all through January.
July 14 is France's national day, with parades and fireworks. On April 1, children stick paper fish on people's backs: "Poisson d'avril !"

Québec celebrates its Fête nationale on June 24 and goes to the cabane à sucre for maple syrup in spring. In Belgium, Saint Nicolas brings children presents on December 6. In Senegal, Tabaski is one of the biggest celebrations of the year.

tips.title: Culture: mistakes foreigners make
body: Use vous with strangers, shop staff, older people and at work, until someone suggests "on peut se tutoyer ?".

False friends: for "I'm excited" say "j'ai hâte", because "je suis excité" can sound awkward. For "I'm full" say "je n'ai plus faim", not "je suis plein". A "librairie" is a bookshop; a library is a "bibliothèque".
Invited to dinner? Arriving 10 to 15 minutes late is polite, but be on time for work. Bring flowers or wine, but never chrysanthemums: they're for funerals.

tips.title: Culture: verlan, Québec and the Belgian numbers
body: Verlan flips the syllables of a word: fou becomes "ouf" (crazy), louche becomes "chelou" (shady, weird), bizarre becomes "zarbi".
In Québec, "c'est plate" means it's boring, a car is "un char" and "tiguidou" means everything's perfect.
Belgium and Switzerland say "septante" (70) and "nonante" (90), and parts of Switzerland say "huitante" (80), instead of France's soixante-dix and quatre-vingt-dix.
Keep slang for friends: "trop bien", "ouf" and "on y go" are perfect with them, not in a job interview.
